parts: Why not just fit a bivariate normal distribution to observed variables x and y? This would be quite straightforward, as it only requires you to estimate mu_x, mu_y, var_x, var_y, and covar_xy (or rho_xy, see manual for examples on how to best parameterise a MVN distribution, although it matters very little for the bivariate case). The slope of the line you are looking for is simply var_y / var_x. In linear regression (where we assume x is observed without error), the slope of the line is also var_y / var_x, but multiplied by rho_xy so as to account for the assumption of x being observed without error (see Wikipedia).

parts:
Let’s focus on your first model — your second model needs a hierarchical
structure and you should play around with the simple hierarchical models
in the manual before attempting it.  Also your second model seems to assume
that our normal distributions are specified in terms of (mean, precision) when
they are really specified in terms of (mean, standard deviation).

Firstly, you need to constrain sigma_x to be positive to be a well-defined
deviation.  Secondly you need priors on everything, not just the x’s.  For
example, if the x’s are all O(1) then 

mu_x ~ normal(0, 5);
sigma_x ~ cauchy(0, 2.5);

will be weakly informative — just informative enough to ensure O(1).

theta is going to be trickier as there may be reflection degeneracies
in your model.  If you can ensure that theta is within that window then
I’d do something like

parameters {
  real theta_tilde;
}

transformed parameters {
  real theta;
  theta <- pi() * (inv_logit(theta_tilde) - 0.5);
}

model {
  theta_tilde ~ normal(0, 5);
}

Make sure that you do something for alpha_perp, too.

Even if you do all of that then there still might be problems because your
model itself may not be sufficiently identified by the data (i.e. that second
mode could be much consistent with the data that you have).  So step
back a bit and build up your model sequentially using simulated data.

1. Start with no measurement error on the x’s.  Simulate data from
    y <- alpha_perp / cos(theta) + sin(theta) * x + noise and see if you
    can recover the simulation parameters theta and alpha_perp.

2. If you can, then add noise to the x’s and see if you can still recover
    the true values.

My guess is that once the x’s become subject to measurement noise
then you’ll run into a non-identifiability where theta -> theta +/- pi, x -> -x.
In this case the multi modality is real and HMC is doing the right thing!
The only way to get rid of the mode is to add more prior information to
make the latent x’s better identified.

parts:
I'm not sure if this is your problem, but you have a potentially
very fat-tailed prior on x and only a single observation x_meas to fit
each parameter x with.

You can also have problems with parameters like B0 that you expect
to be around 53. Stan has to figure that out during adaptation. We
often recommend the non-centered style parameterization of this, where you'd
have

B0_raw ~ normal(0, 1);
B0 <- B0_raw + 53;

And similarly for beta, with

beta_raw ~ normal(0, 1);
beta <- beta_raw * maxSlope;

- Bob

P.S. I find this kind of thing:
B0 + beta *( x -2.)

very hard to read compared to the more standard

B0 + beta * (x - 2)

or even "2.0" in place of "2" (you only need to do that if
all the expressions are integers and you don't want the
rounded down integer result).

be doing. Otherwise, I can run some simulations and try to
track down what's going on if you send us the JAGS model, data
simulator, and your proposed Stan model.

You really want to stay away from those fat gamma priors.
They'll pull your posterior away from where you want it to be.

We also don't recommend hard constraints, like uniform(-5, 5),
but if you insist on using them, you need to make sure the parameters
are declared with <lower=-5, upper=5> so that every value satisfying
the constraints has support (density > 0) in the model.

Also, you have to be careful with the notion of "bias" in a Bayesian
setting. For example, adding a prior to a parameter trades variance
for some bias in finite samples. Same thing happens with
regularization in a penalized MLE setting.

- Bob

Bias compared to what?  There’s no guarantee that any posterior summary (mean, median, etc)
will yield an unbiased estimator with respect to the true data generating process, nor does Bayes
claim on to exist.  

When the measurement error grows then the covariates get washed out, and for all intents and
purposes you’re fitting a constant, which will pull the slope towards zero.  Is that the bias you’re
seeing?  The beta being too small?  Again that is entirely expected when you have measurement
errors that large.

Hopefully someone knows the answer to what this model should

simulator, and your proposed Stan model.  

You really want to stay away from those fat gamma priors.
They'll pull your posterior away from where you want it to be.

We also don't recommend hard constraints, like uniform(-5, 5),
but if you insist on using them, you need to make sure the parameters
are declared with <lower=-5, upper=5> so that every value satisfying
the constraints has support (density > 0) in the model.

Also, you have to be careful with the notion of "bias" in a Bayesian
setting.  For example, adding a prior to a parameter trades variance
for some bias in finite samples.  Same thing happens with
regularization in a penalized MLE setting.

- Bob

You really want to stay away from those fat gamma priors.
They'll pull your posterior away from where you want it to be.

We also don't recommend hard constraints, like uniform(-5, 5),
but if you insist on using them, you need to make sure the parameters
are declared with <lower=-5, upper=5> so that every value satisfying
the constraints has support (density > 0) in the model.

Also, you have to be careful with the notion of "bias" in a Bayesian
setting.  For example, adding a prior to a parameter trades variance
for some bias in finite samples.  Same thing happens with
regularization in a penalized MLE setting.

- Bob

parts: The beta is too small. So it is being pulled toward zero. I've seen more advanced approaches to this (Kelly (2007) if you are familiar) that nail beta well with the same data.... but there is a growing bias in beta towards zero. I wouldn’t say it’s depressing — it’s a proper quantification of uncertainty which should
be exciting!  Ultimately you don’t want to compare any posterior-derived point estimate 
of beta to the truth but rather the entire posterior distribution.  For example, it’s a much
fairer comparison to see if a 90% credible interval (between the 5% and 95% quantiles)
